items.context:
A slide says: "Sculley and colleagues showed that less than 10% of the code
in a production ML system is the model." The link they cite returns HTTP
200.

What does the paper actually say?
items.why:
Invented precision that accreted through repetition. This is why the course
insists on two separate checks, and the second is the one people skip: the
URL resolves, *and* the page contains the claim you are citing it for. A
200 is evidence of the first only. The underlying point survives without
the number, which is exactly why the number was never needed.
items.true: The figure does not appear in the paper; it says only that the ML code box is tiny in proportion to the rest of the system
false: Under 5%, so the slide has rounded in the wrong direction
10% of engineering effort rather than of code, so the units are wrong
It appears in the appendix, so the claim is right but under-cited

items.context:
Public Health England, September 2020. Test results were consolidated into
Excel templates in the legacy `.xls` format, which caps a worksheet at
65,536 rows.

What happened when a file hit the ceiling?
items.why:
15,841 positive cases went unreported for a week, and the contacts of those
people were not traced. No exception, no alert, no partial record to
notice: the failure mode was silence. This is the course's opening argument
in one incident. The model was not the problem, there was no model; the
problem was a data pipeline with a capacity limit and no check that what
went in came out.
items.true: The remaining rows were not rejected with an error; they were simply absent
false: The import failed with an error, and the backlog was reprocessed once the format was changed
The file was split automatically, and the second part was processed a day late
The rows were truncated to fit, so partial records entered the system

items.context:
Google Flu Trends screened 50 million candidate queries down to 45 and
reported a mean correlation of 0.97 across nine regions, on held-out data
excluded from every prior modeling step.

Before you look: was the validation protocol the problem?
items.why:
This is the uncomfortable one, and it is why the case is in the notes.
Held-out validation was done properly and the system still degraded, because
the world changed underneath it: search behavior was not a stable proxy for
influenza, and the relationship the model learned did not survive. Validating
well is not evidence that a system works. It is evidence that it worked on
data you already had.
items.true: No. The protocol was more disciplined than a great deal of deployed machine learning gets, and it still failed in production
false: Yes; screening 50 million candidates guarantees spurious correlations survive to the held-out set
Yes; nine regions is too few to support a correlation estimate
No, and the failure was purely an infrastructure outage rather than a modeling issue

items.context:
Engineering data differs from the datasets in a general ML tutorial in a way
that changes what you have to build. What is the difference?
items.why:
Size and noise are real and neither is the distinguishing property. What
makes engineering data different is that somebody may later have to
establish which instrument produced a number, when it was calibrated, and
what the model recommended on the basis of it. That is a requirement about
records rather than about accuracy, and no amount of model quality
substitutes for it.
items.true: It carries provenance and traceability requirements, because the outputs feed decisions with physical and safety consequences
false: It is larger, so the tooling has to scale further than a tutorial's does
It is noisier, so more of the effort goes into cleaning than into modeling
It is proprietary, so it cannot be shared and every project starts from scratch

items.context:
The 737 MAX case is often summarized as "the software was buggy."

What do the investigations say about the sensor architecture?
items.why:
The generalisable shape is not about aircraft. A system that acts on one
input has no way to notice that the input is wrong, so the failure is in the
architecture rather than in the code that ran correctly on bad data. Ask of
your own systems what a single wrong sensor reading would do, and whether
anything downstream could tell.
items.true: That the system acted on a single angle-of-attack sensor, so one faulty input had no contradiction available
false: That redundant sensors were fitted and the voting logic failed to use them
That the sensors were correct and the fault lay entirely in pilot training
That sensor data was corrupted in transit between the vane and the flight computer

items.context:
The course standardizes on `uv` for environments. What failure is that
choice preventing?
items.why:
Speed and caching are real and neither is why it is in the toolchain. Every
tool in this course is chosen against a named failure, and this one is
"your figure disagrees with your notebook and neither file records why".
L13 has that failure on the page: scikit-learn 1.8 and 1.9 assign folds
differently under an identical call, and only a lockfile makes that
visible.
items.true: A result that cannot be rebuilt, because a lockfile pins what was actually installed rather than what was requested
false: Slow installs, since uv resolves and downloads faster than the alternatives
Dependency conflicts, which uv resolves where pip would fail
Disk usage, since uv shares a global cache between projects

stack.brief: A month of sensor readings, a model that flags anomalies, and a request to put it in front of people who are not you. Fill every layer, then deploy.

layers.case: Three clinical trials used a flawed analysis nobody could re-run.

options.because: The resolver is free to pick whatever is newest within the loose constraints

layers.case: 15,841 positive cases fell off the end of a spreadsheet.

options.because: A spreadsheet or a CSV file has no opinion about what belongs in a cell

layers.case: 386 degrees Celsius, recorded in good faith by a mote with a dying battery.

options.because: the cleaning rules are written down as queries anyone can read rather than buried in a one-off script
which settings produced this particular number
is the right answer far less often than people expect

layers.case: A fresh checkout broke three times: a missing version, an unpinned seed, an absolute path.

options.because: a much stronger guarantee than a requirements.txt

workloads.text: Readings arrive continuously while several dashboards query them at once.

Storage.because: Writing one row at a time while several consumers read concurrently is a relational problem

workloads.text: One channel, scanned across ten years of history, on a laptop.

Storage.because: close to the worst possible layout for the analytical pattern of scanning a single column across the entire history

requires.because: MLflow will record whatever you log. That includes a run whose environment was never locked and whose seed was never pinned.
The lockfile says nothing about the system C libraries

epilogue.text: Locking the environment, pinning the seed, and tracking the run will then reproduce the *wrong* answer, every time, with perfect fidelity

items.context:
Where does most of the engineering effort in a deployed ML system actually
go?
items.why:
This is the claim the whole course is organized around, and the reason the
first four weeks are about storage and pipelines rather than about models.
The two case studies in this session make the same point from opposite
directions: one system failed with no model in it at all, and the other had
a well-validated model and failed anyway.
items.true: Into the data infrastructure, the evaluation, and the operational practice around the model
false: Into model selection and hyperparameter tuning, which is where accuracy is won
Into inference optimization, since serving cost dominates the lifetime budget
Into user interface work, since adoption determines whether a model delivers value

sequence.prompt: Name the stages of an engineering ML system, in the order the lecture names them.
sequence.why: That is the order the lecture names them in. What is not worth believing is that the work runs left to right: reading it as a linear process is the first thing the notes tell you to unlearn. Real systems iterate hard between features and evaluation, and monitoring feeds back into acquisition the moment drift shows up in production.

terms.prompt: Stages of an engineering ML system

items.context:
Open [`l01-reproducibility.ipynb`](../lectures/l01/l01-reproducibility.ipynb)
and run it top to bottom. It is deliberately defective.

One cell fails for you and a different one fails for your neighbor. Why?
items.why:
`np.trapz` was removed in NumPy 2.0 and `np.trapezoid` was added there, so
exactly one cell fails whichever version you installed, and comparing
failures with a neighbor is the discussion. The absolute path is one of
the other two deliberate defects and it fails for everybody, which is why it
is the less interesting one: a defect that only fires on some machines is
the kind that reaches production.
items.true: It integrates a curve twice, once with `np.trapz` and once with `np.trapezoid`, and exactly one exists in your NumPy version
false: Random seeds differ between machines, so the split is different
The absolute path only exists on the author's machine, so everyone fails identically there
Cell execution order differs, so the failure depends on how you ran it

items.context:
Your model's accuracy is unchanged on the test set, but users report it has
got worse over the last quarter.

What is the most likely explanation, and where does the response belong?
items.why:
This is Google Flu Trends in miniature, and it is why "validating well is
not evidence that a system works" is a section heading rather than an
aside. A frozen test set is exactly right for comparing versions and tells
you nothing about whether the world it was drawn from still exists. L23
turns this into instrumentation.
items.true: The world moved and the frozen test set did not, so the response is monitoring the input distribution rather than re-scoring the same data
false: The users are wrong; a stable test score means stable behavior
The model has degraded numerically, so retraining on the same data will restore it
The test set has leaked into training, which inflates the score while real performance falls

items.context:
"We locked the environment, pinned the seed, and tracked the run, so the
result is trustworthy."

What does that argument miss?
items.why:
Reproducibility makes a result *checkable*; it is a precondition for
catching errors, not a substitute for doing so. Note how the Duke errors
were actually caught: not by re-running the original code, which would have
reproduced its mistakes, but by outside statisticians re-implementing the
analysis from scratch and finding the two disagreed. Reproduction confirms
you can regenerate a number. Confirming it is right is a separate act
called validation.
items.true: Reproducible is not the same as correct: a pipeline with an off-by-one error will reproduce the wrong answer with perfect fidelity
false: Nothing, provided the lockfile is regenerated whenever a dependency changes
Seeds do not make a result reproducible across platforms, so the claim overstates what pinning buys
Tracking is only meaningful if the tracked run is also deployed, which this does not say

items.context:
A lockfile pins the exact version of every Python package. What does it
still not pin?
items.why:
A package version is not the same as the code that runs. The lockfile says
nothing about system C libraries, the CUDA toolkit, or the operating system,
and a pinned version can even become unavailable if it is removed from the
index. For most engineering work that is enough; when you need the whole
stack frozen the tool is a container, which is a Week 12 topic. The honest
framing is that `uv` gives you a reproducible Python environment, which is
most of what you need and not quite all of it.
items.true: The compiled bytes: platform-specific wheels differ between macOS and Linux, and system C libraries are not covered at all
false: The random seed, which has to be set separately in code
Transitive dependencies, which resolve freshly on each install
The Python interpreter version, which is recorded separately

sequence.prompt: The uv commands of a normal day, in the order you reach for them.
sequence.why: init creates the project, add resolves and locks a dependency, run executes inside the environment after checking the lockfile still matches pyproject.toml, and sync rebuilds the whole thing from the lockfile on a machine that has never seen it. The last one is the one that ends "works on my machine".

items.context:
Twenty minutes of poking at a file to decide whether an idea is worth
pursuing. Should you set up a locked, tracked, packaged project first?
items.why:
There is a real judgment call about when to pay for the discipline. Full
scaffolding on a twenty-minute exploration is cumbersome and is its own kind
of over-engineering. The moment an analysis will be rerun, shared, built
upon, or believed by anyone, including your future self, it has crossed the
line, and almost nobody notices the crossing at the time. So the default
leans toward scaffolding, because retrofitting is the expensive direction.
items.true: No for a genuinely throwaway exploration, but the trap is that results cross the line into needing it quietly
false: Yes, always; the discipline is cheap and retrofitting is expensive
No; scaffolding is only warranted once a result is going to be published
Yes, because an unlocked environment cannot produce a result worth acting on at all

items.context:
A content hash tells you two runs used different data. What does it not
tell you?
items.why:
A hash is a smoke alarm, not an investigation. Detecting change is the
floor of data provenance rather than the ceiling, and the tools that go
further, versioning data by content with a readable history of what changed
and why, are `git-lfs` and DVC. Collisions are not the concern: the hash is
certain that the file differs, and useless about everything after that.
items.true: Which rows changed, whether the change was a fix or a corruption, or whether it matters
false: Whether the file is genuinely different, since hashes collide in practice
When the change happened, which requires a timestamp alongside the hash
Who made the change, which requires an audit log rather than a hash

items.context:
Every run in your MLflow project logs a seed. A colleague concludes the
project is reproducible.

What is wrong with that inference?
items.why:
The tracker is a filing system, and a filing system is only as trustworthy
as the discipline of the person filing. Logging a seed documents one input
to a run that may still be irreproducible for a dozen other reasons. The
third option is a real and separate concern; it is not the flaw in the
inference, which is that recording is being mistaken for guaranteeing.
items.true: Tracking records, it does not enforce: MLflow will faithfully log a run whose environment was never locked
false: Nothing; a logged seed plus logged parameters is what reproducibility means in practice
Seeds are per-library, so one logged seed does not cover NumPy, PyTorch and Python's own RNG
The seed should be logged as a tag rather than a parameter, or it will not be searchable

items.context: Why do large binary files not belong in plain git?
items.why:
Code, data, and models are three different versioning problems and the
session is explicit that one tool does not serve all three. Git is superb
for text it can diff and terrible for a 400 MB file rewritten weekly,
because every version stays in the history forever. That the diffs are
uninformative is true and is not the binding cost; the binding cost is that
the repository stops being clonable.
items.true: Git stores a full copy of every version, so a repeatedly-changed binary makes the history unusable to clone
false: Git rejects files above a fixed size limit, so they cannot be committed at all
Git cannot compute diffs for binary content, so the commits carry no information
Binary files break the working tree on checkout across operating systems

items.context:
What is the point of turning an exploratory notebook into a module with a
command-line entry point?
items.why:
Notebooks are version-controllable, awkwardly, so that is not the argument.
The argument is that a notebook's execution order is a human decision made
at runtime, and a module's is not. Once there is an entry point, CI can run
it, a scheduler can run it, and a test can assert what it produces, none of
which is available to a sequence of cells.
items.true: It becomes testable and callable, so the thing you validated can be run again by something other than a human clicking cells
false: Speed, since a script runs faster than the same code in a notebook kernel
Notebooks cannot be version-controlled, so moving to a script is what makes the work reviewable
It reduces memory use, since a script releases state between stages

sequence.prompt: The notebook refactor: the functions the data moves through, in order.
sequence.why: The refactor is mechanical, which is the good news. Each function takes its inputs as arguments and returns a value, so it can be imported and tested on its own rather than depending on the ambient state of a notebook that has to be run in an order you remember.

terms.prompt: Folders and files of the src layout

items.context:
Two labs report different results from what is supposedly the same
analysis. Both can reproduce their own numbers exactly.

What resolves it?
items.why:
Every other option is a good diagnostic and none of them can catch a shared
misunderstanding of what the analysis should do. Re-running reproduces;
re-implementing validates. The Duke errors survived because re-running the
original code would have faithfully regenerated the mistakes, and they were
only found when outside statisticians built the analysis again from scratch
and the two versions disagreed.
items.true: Re-implementing the analysis independently, which is how the Duke errors were actually found
false: Comparing lockfiles, since a dependency difference is the likeliest cause of a numeric disagreement
Re-running each pipeline on the other lab's data, which isolates data from code
Increasing precision, since disagreements of this kind usually trace to floating-point accumulation

items.context:
Open [`l02-scaffold.ipynb`](../lectures/l02/l02-scaffold.ipynb) and work
through building the project scaffold.

What does `uv` produce that a `requirements.txt` does not?
items.why:
A requirements file is a request; a lockfile is a record. The distinction
only bites when a transitive dependency moves under you, which is exactly
the failure L13 documents when scikit-learn 1.8 and 1.9 assigned folds
differently under an identical call. Speed is real and is not the reason
this is in the toolchain.
items.true: A lockfile recording what was actually installed, including transitive dependencies, rather than what was asked for
false: A faster install, since uv resolves dependencies in parallel
A virtual environment, which requirements.txt cannot create
A dependency graph, which requirements.txt flattens and loses

items.context:
```sql
SELECT * FROM readings WHERE value <> 30;
```
Your sensor table has nulls in `value`. What does this return?
items.why:
SQL has three truth values, not two: true, false, and unknown. "Unknown is
not equal to 30" evaluates to unknown rather than to true, so the row is
not returned. This is defined semantics rather than a defect, and it
quietly produces wrong analyses for anyone who forgets it. The same family
contains a worse one: `NOT IN` against a subquery containing a single null
returns no rows at all.
items.true: Every row whose value is not 30, silently excluding all null rows
false: Every row whose value is not 30, including the null ones, since null is not 30
An error, since a comparison against null is not permitted in a WHERE clause
Every row, since null comparisons default to true in PostgreSQL

items.context:
A mote dropped half its readings. You compute `avg(value)` over its rows.
What do you get?
items.why:
`count(*)` counts rows while `count(value)` counts only non-null ones, and
`avg(value)` averages only the readings that are present. So the mote is
not penalized in the average unless you have separately counted how many it
reported. The habit worth forming is to carry a completeness count next to
any aggregate over sensor data, because the aggregate alone cannot tell you
whether it summarizes everything or half of it.
items.true: An average over the readings that are present, with the missing ones simply absent from it
false: An average that treats missing readings as zero, biasing it downward
Null, because any aggregate over a column containing nulls is null
An error, unless the nulls are filtered out first

items.context:
Your experiment metadata records a different, unpredictable set of fields
for every run. You are putting it in PostgreSQL and the schema keeps
changing.

What does that tell you?
items.why:
The same schema that protected your readings table is expensive to change
once it is large, and a migration against a nine-million-row table in a live
deployment is a real operation with real risk. Heterogeneous metadata is the
case where rigidity stops paying, and recognizing it is the point: the
relational model is a default, not a universal answer. A JSON column is a
genuine option and it is the relational model conceding the argument rather
than winning it.
items.true: That this is exactly the territory where the rigid schema stops helping and document stores earn their place
false: That the schema needs a JSON column, which restores flexibility inside the relational model
That the runs should be normalized further, into a table per field type
That migrations should be automated, since the schema churn is a tooling problem

items.context:
Why store sensor data long (one row per reading) rather than wide (one
column per sensor)?
items.why:
A wide table encodes your current instrument list into the schema, so
commissioning a sensor becomes a migration and decommissioning one leaves a
column of nulls forever. Long tables decouple the two. The cost is real and
worth knowing: queries that want several channels side by side now need a
pivot or a join, which is why the session spends time on window functions
and time bucketing.
items.true: Adding a sensor is a new row rather than a schema change, and the schema stops depending on which instruments exist
false: Long tables compress better, so the storage cost is lower at scale
Long tables are faster to query, since the index fits in memory
Wide tables cannot represent timestamps consistently across sensors

items.context:
"We used a timestamp column, so the times are correct."

What did 30 June 2012 demonstrate?
items.why:
The case is in the notes because a type that carries physical meaning has
to cope with how the physical quantity actually behaves, and time is the one
everybody assumes is simple. Timezones are a real hazard and a different
one. The general shape is the session's argument about types: a column
declared with the right type is carrying a claim about the world, and the
world occasionally declines to cooperate.
items.true: That a leap second is a real event a timestamp type has to survive, and systems assuming fixed-length days failed
false: That timezone conversion is the main hazard, and UTC storage solves it
That NTP drift accumulates faster than most systems account for
That millisecond precision is insufficient for high-rate sensor data

items.context:
When should a measured quantity be stored as `numeric` rather than
`double precision`?
items.why:
"Always" is the tempting answer and it is wrong: `numeric` is materially
slower and most sensor readings are approximate measurements of a
continuous quantity, where double precision is the honest representation.
The session is also blunt that this does not save you from floating point
elsewhere: a value read into Python as a float is a float again, whatever
the column said.
items.true: When exactness at the stored precision matters more than arithmetic speed, for instance for money or a regulated tolerance
false: Always, since numeric is exact and double precision is approximate
When the values span many orders of magnitude, which double precision handles poorly
Never for sensor data, since numeric cannot represent scientific notation

terms.prompt: Types this schema uses for engineering data

items.context:
A column is declared `double precision NOT NULL`. A reading arrives as
-9999, the instrument's error sentinel.

What happens?
items.why:
The type says "this is a number that is present". It says nothing about
whether the number is physically possible. Sentinels like -9999 are
extremely common in instrument data and they pass every type check, which
is why the session insists on `CHECK` constraints for range and on
validation as a separate layer. This is the same lesson as the units
assertion in L7: the declaration is not the check.
items.true: It is stored, because a typed column is still not a validated column
false: The insert is rejected, since -9999 is outside any plausible physical range
It is coerced to null, since the sentinel is recognized by the driver
It is stored and flagged, since PostgreSQL tracks out-of-range values

sequence.prompt: Loading a sensor export that resists the loader, through a staging table.
steps: COPY the raw text into a permissive table
insert into the real readings table
sequence.why: The point of the staging table is that the cleaning rules end up written down as queries anyone can read, rather than buried in a one-off script. Some of them you do not have to write at all: the foreign key to sensors rejects the corrupt mote ids for you the moment you try to insert one.

items.context:
A time-range query over a large readings table is slow. You add an index
and it is still slow.

What tells you why?
items.why:
Every other option is a real diagnostic and each answers a narrower
question. The plan is the one that tells you what the database actually
decided to do, which is frequently not what you assumed when you added the
index: a predicate that wraps the column in a function, or a range broad
enough that a sequential scan is genuinely cheaper, both produce a
correctly-ignored index.
items.true: The query plan, from `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, which shows whether the index was used and what it cost
false: The table statistics, which show whether the index is selective enough to help
The query duration across repeated runs, which distinguishes cold cache from a bad plan
The index size on disk, which indicates whether it fits in memory

items.context:
Open [`l03-sql-timeseries.ipynb`](../lectures/l03/l03-sql-timeseries.ipynb)
and run the same range query with and without the index, reading the plan
each time.

What changes in the plan?
items.why:
An index that exists and an index that is used are different things, and
the plan is the only place the difference is visible. This is the same
discipline as the rest of the course: the artifact exists is not the same
claim as the artifact works, and you check by looking at what actually
happened rather than at what you configured.
items.true: The scan type changes, and the plan shows whether the index was actually chosen rather than merely present
false: Only the timing; the plan is identical because the planner is deterministic
The row estimates change, since an index updates the table statistics
Nothing visible; index use is reported only in the server log

items.context:
Records in your system are constantly corrected one at a time. Someone
proposes storing them as Parquet for the analytics speedup.

What is wrong with that?
items.why:
The layout that makes analytical scans fast makes changes slow. Column
stores lose the point write, and that is a property to respect rather than
a defect to engineer around: data that is constantly corrected belongs in
the row store from L3. Batching helps and does not change the shape of the
argument, which is about matching the store to the access pattern.
items.true: A Parquet file is effectively immutable: there is no in-place update, so a single correction rewrites the file that holds it
false: Nothing, provided the corrections are batched nightly rather than applied individually
Parquet cannot represent the schema changes that corrections imply
Parquet loses precision on repeated rewrites, so corrections accumulate error

items.context:
"After that lecture, we should replace PostgreSQL with DuckDB and Parquet."

What is wrong with this conclusion?
items.why:
PostgreSQL absorbs the live writes with its schema and transactions intact,
and the history is periodically written out as Parquet that DuckDB scans.
The skill is not loyalty to a column store or a row store; it is placing each
part of the workload where its access pattern is cheap, and moving data
across the seam deliberately.
items.true: It is named in the notes as the most common mistake after the lecture: the two compose, and a real platform runs both
false: Nothing; for analytical workloads the replacement is the recommended migration
DuckDB cannot read PostgreSQL, so the migration would lose the existing data
Parquet lacks the type system to represent what a relational schema encodes

items.context: What is DuckDB not?
items.why:
DuckDB runs inside one process, which is both its convenience and its
boundary: superb for one analyst's laptop, one pipeline's transform step,
one service's embedded analytics, and not trying to be a concurrent
multi-writer server. When several writers need a single consistent view,
that is the relational server's job, and DuckDB complements it rather than
trying to replace it.
items.true: A shared transactional backend that many clients write to concurrently with isolation guarantees
false: An analytical engine, since it is optimized for point lookups rather than scans
A SQL engine, since it uses its own dialect rather than standard SQL
Usable without a server, since it requires a background process to hold state

items.context:
Columnar storage gives a large measured speedup on analytical scans.

Before you look: at what data size does that advantage appear?
items.why:
The measured 80-times speedup appears at millions of rows. Below that scale
a pandas `groupby` is simpler, fast enough, and one fewer moving part, and
reaching for the columnar machinery is over-engineering, the same lesson L2
made about scaffolding a throwaway script. Match the tool to the size as
well as to the access pattern.
items.true: At millions of rows; it shrinks at a few hundred thousand and vanishes on data that fits in memory
false: At a few thousand rows, since the layout advantage is structural rather than a matter of scale
Only above a billion rows, below which the formats are indistinguishable
At any size, though the factor grows with row count

items.context: Why does a column store accelerate an analytical scan?
items.why:
Compression is a genuine second-order benefit and it follows from the same
property: values in a column are homogeneous, so they compress far better
than a row of mixed types. But the primary mechanism is that the layout
lets you skip what you did not ask for, and that is why the advantage is
about access pattern rather than about size alone.
items.true: A query touching three of forty columns reads only those three, instead of every row in full
false: It compresses better, so less data has to be read from disk overall
It keeps an index on every column, so any predicate can be answered from an index
It stores data pre-aggregated, so common groupings are already computed

items.context:
A colleague wants a document store because designing the schema is taking
too long.

Is that a good reason?
items.why:
Document, key-value, and time-series stores each solve a real problem by
giving something up, and what they give up is usually the relational
contract from L3: the enforced schema, the joins, the transactions. That is
the right trade when the data genuinely does not fit a table, and a bad one
when it is a way of not deciding. The fourth option is wrong in a different
direction: they are not slower everywhere, they are faster at the pattern
they were built for.
items.true: No. Choose one because your access pattern demands it, not because a schema felt like work
false: Yes; schema design is a bottleneck and document stores let it be deferred until the shape settles
Yes, provided a schema is imposed later at the application layer
No, because document stores are slower than relational databases at every access pattern

items.context: Which store fits "continuous writes, point lookups, strong consistency"?
items.why:
The rule the whole arc is building toward: store data in the shape that
matches how it will be read. Continuous writes, point lookups and strong
consistency say row store; wide scans and aggregates over history say
column store. A document store does point lookups well and gives up the
consistency guarantee, which is exactly the part this question specified.
items.true: A row store and OLTP, which is the relational database of L3
false: A column store with Parquet files, since the writes can be appended as new files
A document store, since point lookups by key are its core operation
A time-series database, since it is built for high-rate timestamped writes

items.context:
A pipeline writes one Parquet file per reading, as readings arrive.

What is wrong?
items.why:
Writing new files is indeed how you add data to Parquet, which is what makes
this failure plausible enough to happen: the mechanism is correct and the
granularity destroys the point. Columnar compression and column skipping
both need many rows in one file to do anything, and each file carries schema
and footer overhead. This access pattern is a row store's, and it should be
in one.

items.context:
You publish every mote's readings to one Kafka topic with several
partitions.

What does Kafka promise about the order you read them back in?
items.why:
Kafka appends each event to one partition, and a consumer reads each
partition forward in the order events were appended. There is no
guarantee across partitions. If you need one mote's readings in order,
they have to land in the same partition. Kafka also knows nothing about
event time: append order is not the order the readings were measured.

false: Order across the whole topic

items.context:
A consumer reads flow readings from Kafka with default settings and adds
each one to a running total of product shipped.

What will eventually make the total wrong?
items.why:
Kafka is at-least-once by default: a message is never lost, but it can
arrive more than once. A running sum is not idempotent, so every
redelivery inflates it. Exactly-once is opt-in machinery rather than a
setting on the cluster, so assume duplicates and make the processing
tolerate them, for example by de-duplicating on a message id.
items.true: A redelivered message gets counted twice
false: A message is lost and never delivered

items.context: What is a watermark in a streaming pipeline?
items.why:
A watermark is the system's estimate that it has now seen every event up
to some event time, and when it passes the end of a window the window
closes and emits. It is usually a heuristic, so it can be wrong: a
reading can still turn up after its window closed. That is late data,
and the pipeline needs a policy for it.
items.true: A guess that events up to some time have arrived
false: A guarantee that no later event will ever arrive
The processing time at which a window was emitted
The timestamp of the newest event seen so far

items.context:
On single runs of reactor pressure, 30 minutes ahead, a random forest scores
4.32 kPa under shuffled KFold and 6.92 kPa under TimeSeriesSplit. Persistence
scores about 6.1. What should you report?
items.why:
Shuffled, each test row has neighbours from before and after it in training,
and a forest recalls them. The time-ordered score is the one you would see in
use, and it is worse than persistence.
items.true: The forest loses to persistence, so do not use it
false: The forest beats persistence by about 30 %
The average of the two scores, about 5.6 kPa
Neither, because the two splits disagree

items.context:
Pooled over 200 independent runs, a ridge model scores 4.74 kPa on a shuffled
row split and 4.71 kPa split by run. A classmate concludes the notes were wrong
about shuffling. What is the better reading?
items.why:
With that much data a linear model barely leans on a test row's few
neighbours, and K-fold is valid for a purely autoregressive model with
uncorrelated errors. The shuffled score is most dangerous on one short series
with a flexible model, where it flattered two models past persistence.
items.true: Never shuffling is a safe default, and this case sits at its boundary
false: Shuffling is always safe for linear models on any series
The by-run split must contain a bug
The runs must share neighbouring rows

items.context:
A residual detector alarms whenever a residual exceeds the 99th percentile of
normal residuals. The plant logs one sample every three minutes. Roughly how
many false alarms a day should you expect?
items.why:
The 99th percentile is exceeded by 1 % of normal samples by construction, and
a day holds 480 three-minute samples. Operators learn to ignore a detector that
cries wolf five times a day.
items.true: About 4.8
false: About 0.01
About 48
About 0.48

items.context:
After fault 1 begins, the one-step residual on reactor pressure leaves its
normal band, then returns inside it hours later, while the fault is still
present. Why?
items.why:
A residual reacts to surprise, not to distance from normal. Once the plant
settles into a new steady state, a one-step model predicts it well again, and
from the pressure channel alone nothing looks wrong.
items.true: The controller compensated, so the new state looks normal on this channel
false: The fault cleared itself partway through the run
The threshold was recalculated during the run
The model was retrained on the faulty data

items.context:
You want fewer false alarms from a residual detector, so you require three
consecutive exceedances before alarming. What do you give up?
items.why:
Lowering the false-alarm rate raises the detection delay. Three in a row
cannot fire until the third sample, so every alarm comes at least six minutes
later, and later still for a residual that flickers across the threshold.
items.true: Every fault is detected later
false: The threshold no longer comes from normal data
The detector can no longer run without fault examples
Nothing, since false alarms and delay are unrelated

items.context:
The concrete dataset has 1,030 rows: seven ingredient amounts, the age in
days, and the compressive strength in MPa. What is one sample?
items.why:
A sample is one row, and each row is one mix crushed at one age. The same mix
crushed at 7 and at 28 days is two samples, which is why the rows are not all
independent experiments.
items.true: One concrete mix tested at one age
false: One concrete mix, across every age it was tested at
One ingredient amount in one mix
One strength value, with its units

items.context:
In Lecture 8, shuffling the rows before splitting let a forecaster read the
future. On the water and surfactant data, shuffling the rows before splitting
is allowed. What changed?
items.why:
A time series has an order that decides what counts as the future. A table of
separate experiments does not. The catch is that separate rows are not always
separate experiments: the 1,030 concrete rows are 428 mixes, which is why the
concrete test set and folds are split by mix with GroupKFold.
items.true: The rows are separate experiments, so their order in the file means nothing
false: The water and surfactant data are small, so leakage is too small to matter
Regression models cannot use the order of the rows
The target is measured at the same time as the features, so it cannot leak

items.context:
A student fits a network, scores it on the test set, adds four hidden units
because the score looked low, and scores it on the test set again. They report
the second test score. What is wrong?
items.why:
Changing the model because of a test score lets information from the test rows
into the choice. After that the test set is doing the validation set's job, and
the number it gives is optimistic. The test set is touched once.
items.true: The test set has become validation data, so its score no longer estimates new data
false: Nothing; the test set was only used to check the model, never to fit it
The network needed a larger training set, not more hidden units
Test scores should be averaged over both attempts before reporting

items.context:
A tanh network is trained on two inputs, x1 between 0 and 1 and x2 between 0 and
1,000,000, with no scaling. It scores R-squared = -0.006 on test data. Why?
items.why:
With x2 in the millions, every unit's weighted sum is huge, so tanh sits at plus or
minus 1 on every training row and its gradient vanishes. The network can then fit
only a constant, the training mean, which is why R-squared lands just below zero
rather than far below it. Standardizing both inputs puts them on equal footing, and
the same network reaches 0.9999.
items.true: Every tanh unit saturates, so the gradients vanish and it predicts the training mean
false: A network cannot combine two inputs measured in different units, so it gives up on both of them
The x2 input is irrelevant to y, so the network ignores it and underfits x1
The weights diverge on the huge x2 values, so the predictions grow without bound

items.context:
A GP fitted on the 21 water points between 0 and 100 C is asked about 300 C,
where NIST gives 517.7 MPa. What does its plus-or-minus-two-standard-deviation
band do there?
items.why:
A GP's uncertainty grows with distance from the data, under the kernel's
assumption about smoothness. It knows nothing about physics the data never
showed it, so a wide band can still miss the truth.
items.true: It grows to about 232 MPa either side and still misses the NIST value
false: It grows wide enough that the NIST value falls inside it
It stays as narrow as it is inside the data, since the kernel is smooth
It shrinks to zero, because the mean returns to the training average

items.context:
A learning curve for a linear model ends with training RMSE 7.16 MPa and
validation RMSE 7.43 MPa, and the two curves have met. On the same folds, a model
with more capacity reaches a validation RMSE of 6.06 MPa. What is the diagnosis?
items.why:
The gap between the curves is the variance, and it has closed to 0.3 MPa, so more
samples can buy at most that much. Even then, validation would sit near 7.2 MPa,
while a model with more capacity already reaches 6.06 on the same folds. The level
where the curves meet is the bias, so the line is too simple for the relationship.
Curves that meet are a good fit only when no other model does clearly better.
items.true: Underfitting: it needs more capacity or better features, not more samples
false: Overfitting: it needs regularization or a smaller model to close the gap
A good fit: the curves have met, so stop tuning and test it once on the test set
A leak: training and validation errors should never be as close as that

items.context:
A GaussianProcessRegressor is fitted on 835 concrete rows. What does its `.fit`
optimize?
items.why:
Given the hyperparameters, the GP's predicted mean and variance are closed-form
linear algebra, a solve with K + noise. What is optimized is the handful of kernel
hyperparameters (ten for the concrete GP), and each evaluation of the objective
factorizes an N by N matrix, which is where the O(N^3) cost comes from.
scikit-learn solves it with L-BFGS-B on the logarithms of the hyperparameters,
inside the kernel's bounds, from several starting points.
items.true: The kernel hyperparameters, by maximizing the log marginal likelihood
false: One weight per training point, by gradient descent on the squared error
The predicted mean at every training point, by least squares
Nothing: a GP is nonparametric, so fit only stores the training rows

items.context:
An NN-NARX forecasts reactor pressure (about 2,705 kPa, standard deviation 7.7 kPa)
30 minutes ahead. The inputs go through a StandardScaler. Its test RMSE is 7.57 kPa,
exactly the score of predicting the mean. What is the most likely defect?
items.why:
The network has to produce numbers near 2,705 from weights that start near zero.
Wrapping it in TransformedTargetRegressor with a StandardScaler scales the target as
well, and the same network then scores 4.73 kPa, tied with the ridge ARX. It is
Lecture 7's deviation variables, applied to the target.
items.true: The target was not scaled, so the network stopped at the mean
false: Ten lags are too few for a forecast 30 minutes ahead
The inputs should not have been standardized for a time series
A network cannot use lag features, only a linear model can

items.context:
You give a model more capacity: a deeper tree, more hidden units, a smaller penalty.
What typically happens to its bias and its variance?
items.why:
More capacity lets the model follow the truth more closely (lower bias) and also
follow the particular training rows more closely (higher variance). The noise term
does not move at all. Validation error is lowest at the capacity where the falling
bias and the rising variance balance.
items.true: Bias goes down and variance goes up
false: Bias goes up and variance goes down
Both go down, which is why larger models win
Both go up, which is why larger models overfit

items.context:
Gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), Adam and L-BFGS are all
variants of one update, `theta_new = theta - eta * H * g`, where g is the gradient
of the loss and H is a matrix that shapes the step. What separates SGD from
L-BFGS in that update?
items.why:
The methods differ in two choices: which rows the gradient comes from, and what H
is. SGD uses the gradient of a small random mini-batch, a noisy estimate of the full
one, and no step shaping, so each step is cheap. L-BFGS uses the exact gradient over
all the rows and builds an estimate of the inverse Hessian from its last few steps.
On the straight-line fit to the water data that took it 6 iterations, against 305
for gradient descent.
items.true: SGD takes g from a random mini-batch and uses the identity for H; L-BFGS uses all the rows and an inverse-Hessian estimate
false: SGD shapes the step with an inverse-Hessian estimate built from recent steps; L-BFGS uses the identity and a random mini-batch
Both use the gradient over all the rows and the identity for H; SGD simply takes a smaller step length eta
SGD computes no gradient at all: it tries random steps and keeps the ones that happen to lower the loss

items.context:
The three-unit network, fitted on 96 rows, is trained with L-BFGS. The NN-NARX,
fitted on 144,300 rows, is trained with Adam, a stochastic method. Why is L-BFGS
the method of choice for the small problem and not for the large one?
items.why:
L-BFGS needs few iterations on a smooth problem, but each one uses the exact gradient
over the whole dataset, and its curvature estimate assumes that gradient is exact. On
small and medium data a full gradient is cheap. On a large table a stochastic method
such as SGD or Adam takes thousands of cheap mini-batch steps in the time one full
gradient would take. L-BFGS keeps only the last few steps, not a full Hessian, and the
three-unit network's loss is itself non-convex.
items.true: Every L-BFGS iteration needs the gradient over all the rows, which is cheap on 96 rows and costly on 144,300
false: L-BFGS stores the full Hessian matrix, so it runs out of memory once a network has more than a few hundred weights
L-BFGS converges only on convex losses, and a larger network's loss is not convex while a small network's is
L-BFGS adds random noise to every step, which averages out over a few rows but not over many thousands

items.context:
In scikit-learn, `MLPRegressor(solver="lbfgs")` and `GaussianProcessRegressor`
both hand their training problem to the same SciPy routine, L-BFGS-B. How do the
two problems differ?
items.why:
The network's lbfgs solver calls L-BFGS-B with no bounds at all, which makes it plain
L-BFGS, and Adam and SGD apply none either, so a weight can take any value. A GP has
no weights. Its decision variables are a handful of kernel hyperparameters, worked on
as logarithms because length scales and variances live on a log scale. Every kernel
carries bounds on them (10^-5 to 10^5 for the RBF length scale by default), and
L-BFGS-B, the version of L-BFGS that handles bounds, enforces them.
items.true: The GP works on the logs of a few kernel hyperparameters, inside bounds; the network's weights are unbounded
false: Both are bounded: every network weight and every GP hyperparameter must stay between 1e-5 and 1e5 throughout training
The network's weights are bounded so that they stay positive; the GP's hyperparameters are free
Neither is bounded; the B in L-BFGS-B only changes how the routine stores its past steps

items.context:
Lecture 8's forecaster predicts reactor pressure 30 minutes ahead from its last ten
measured values, y(t), y(t-3), ..., y(t-27), and the eleven valve positions now, and
Lecture 8 fitted it with ridge. Keep the same table and the same columns, and fit an
MLPRegressor instead. What is the model now?
items.why:
ARX and NARX share the table; they differ in f. With a linear f, as in Lecture 8's
ridge fit, the model is an ARX; with a network or a GP it is a nonlinear ARX. The
inputs are measured past pressures, so no forecast is fed back, and nothing in the
four families needs the rows to be separate experiments.
items.true: A NARX model: the same lagged columns, with a network as the nonlinear f
false: Still an ARX model, since the name describes the lagged columns and not the function fitted to them
A recurrent network, since it now feeds its own forecasts back in as inputs
Not a valid model, since a network needs rows that are separate experiments
